title: Empatica Embrace seizure alert reaches Morgan McGrath's mother, who calls paramedics after a seizure left the 26-year-old teacher not breathing (Fulton, Missouri)
summary: IEEE Spectrum (6 February 2018): an Embrace wristband alerted the mother of Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Mo., during a seizure about 15 months earlier; she called paramedics and McGrath survived.
account: Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018 on Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri. She “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”. The publication date is used because the article dates the seizure only to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics, and “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The article says it records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text or call to pre-specified caregivers. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. A later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021) by Empatica staff with hospital co-authors reports sensitivity for a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. An independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study (Jahani et al. 2026) found the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures while worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on this single news item. The Empatica case-study abstract (Regalia, Onorati, Picard, American Epilepsy Society) is not among the sources. No second account of the McGrath event was found.
purpose: Built to detect convulsive seizures from electrodermal activity and motion and to summon designated caregivers. The alert to McGrath's mother was that purpose.
system: Empatica Embrace wrist-worn seizure detection (electrodermal activity and accelerometer, on-board algorithm) with the Alert smartphone app
model_version: Embrace (the article does not state the generation); echoes concern Embrace2
segment: Prescription wearable seizure monitor used at home

ratings.reason: A young woman not breathing during a seizure had paramedics summoned by her mother on the device's alert and is reported alive and well. A potentially life-saving response documented only in one news report.

ai_role.statement: Per IEEE Spectrum, the Embrace detected the seizure and its app alerted McGrath's mother, who made the emergency call. The device did not call for help itself. The article calls the algorithm proprietary. The FDA summary describes it as an on-board algorithm validated against video-EEG. Empatica's own 2021 study calls it a predefined machine-learning algorithm. The McGrath event is known only from this single news item. The AES case-study abstract is not among the sources.

evidence.quote: Alerts successfully reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with one failure due to a Wi‐Fi disconnection.

produced_by: A convulsive (generalized tonic-clonic) seizure, the only type the device is cleared to detect
The wristband worn and paired with a phone running the Alert app, with a caregiver designated
A caregiver able to reach the patient or call emergency services on receiving the alert
must_hold: Connectivity between watch, phone and caregiver (one of 16 alerts in Montreal failed on a Wi-Fi disconnection)
Caregivers tolerate false alarms (29 in 373 monitoring days in Montreal, mostly from routine movements)
Focal seizures without convulsions are not detected (none of 510 in Montreal)

echoes.setting: Center hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal epilepsy monitoring unit, 72 patients, April 2024 to June 2025; alerts routed to nursing staff
echoes.source: Jahani et al. (2026) Epilepsia 67(4):1802-1816, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13075604/ (quote: 'The Embrace2 wrist‐worn device detected all 16 FBTCSs/GTCSs that occurred while the device was functioning and worn, but none of 510 FSs.')

echoes.setting: Multicentre epilepsy-monitoring-unit study, 152 patients (85 children), 66 convulsive seizures; detection performance only, no home alerts
echoes.source: Onorati et al. (2021) Front Neurol 12:724904, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8418082/ (sensitivity 0.92 pediatric, 0.94 adult; false alarm rate 1.26 and 0.57 per 24 h)

headline: Empatica Embrace seizure alert reaches Morgan McGrath's mother

comparator.against: seizures recorded during more than 6,500 hours of monitoring of 135 patients (device test reported by IEEE Spectrum)
comparator.after: the device correctly identified nearly every single seizure, with a false alarm rate below that of the seizure frequency for most individuals
comparator.quote: When tested on 135 patients who were monitored for a collective total of more than 6,500 hours, the device correctly identified nearly every single seizure, with a false alarm rate below that of the seizure frequency for most individuals.

later.note: An independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study later found the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while worn and working, with alerts reaching caregivers in 15 of 16 cases and 29 false alarms over the study.
later.quote: Alerts successfully reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with one failure due to a Wi‐Fi disconnection.
